strengths: PST addresses a relevant gap in multimodal NLP evaluation: gender associations can change when occupations and organizational roles are depicted together. Crossing occupations and counterbalancing their left/right positions provides a useful evaluation design.

The observational findings have meaningful human support: three annotators assess each target individual, with reported Fleiss’ kappa of 0.88–0.92. The appendices provide occupation lists, generation prompts, annotation instructions, and detailed results.
FairCritic is a practical intervention requiring no generator retraining. Its inspectable feedback and reported reductions in stereotype scores provide promising preliminary evidence.
weaknesses: The fairness conclusions exceed what the metric establishes. Equation 1 averages signed stereotype adherence, so opposing biases can cancel. For example, Table 1’s single-person occupational SS of 10 combines female-stereotyped and male-stereotyped subgroup scores of 50 and −30; this does not establish an approximately unbiased baseline. Similarly, low post-mitigation subgroup averages cannot establish parity within individual occupations. Per-role distributional results and absolute deviations are needed to substantiate 'near-perfect fairness.'

The headline percentage lacks an appropriate reference. Figure 6’s PST(Any) counts an image whenever either person matches a stereotype; an independently gender-balanced generator would satisfy this condition in 75% of two-person images. Consequently, the reported 74.3% alone does not demonstrate unfairness, although the marginal and joint-assignment results provide separate evidence of stereotyped associations.

The single-person baseline uses only three images per identity, making occupation-specific reversals and amplification estimates unstable. The paper provides no confidence intervals or inferential analysis for these comparisons, and no repeated-run uncertainty for FairCritic. The large aggregate occupational shift is more convincing than the finer-grained claims.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified for reproducibility. Section 5.1 and Figure 9 leave the complete critic prompting protocol, image batch size, feedback integration procedure, and mitigation generation/annotation counts unclear. The conflicting totals of 944 and 1,952 evaluation prompts also need reconciliation.

The mitigation comparison does not establish the claimed superiority over prompt interventions. Table 2 evaluates the occupational intervention on selected top-five subsets, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic over the broader evaluation. Both methods should be compared on identical prompts, with sampling budgets disclosed; a fixed-feedback or resampling control would help establish the value of adaptive criticism.

The annotation protocol measures perceived gender without separately verifying that generated people occupy the requested roles and positions. Treatment of 'Cannot Identify' responses and failed generations is unspecified, and prompt fidelity after mitigation is not measured. These omissions leave compositional errors potentially confounded with changes in bias. Together with the metric and mitigation-validation issues, they require substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
